meta.title: Build an Evaluation Harness with promptfoo
meta.thesis: Build an Evaluation Harness with promptfoo is practical when learners can apply it to this concrete case: A policy-answering bot changed prompts and the team needs to catch regressions before release. By the end, they should be able to build or review Promptfoo-style eval suite with golden cases and assertions, measure regression failures caught before deployment, and catch the failure where a prompt update improves tone but drops required policy citations.

modules.title: Write the harness contract and file layout
modules.sub: Make the eval target reviewable before adding cases.
modules.summary: The build starts with files, owners, and release questions.
objectives: Define what the harness must prove.
Choose a small file layout for prompts, cases, and config.
Set pass/fail behavior before writing assertions.

blocks.title: A harness is a release artifact

spans.text: Problem anchor: a policy-answering bot changed prompts and now might drop required citations. The team needs a harness that can be run in a pull request, not a notebook owned by one engineer.

The first artifact is a small repository layout: promptfooconfig.yaml, prompts/policy_v1.txt, prompts/policy_v2.txt, cases/refunds.yaml, scripts/app_target.ts, and docs/eval-triage.md. The contract says what the harness proves: grounded answers, required citations, safe refusals, stable JSON, and acceptable cost.

blocks.title: Worked file layout for the policy bot

items.text: cases/ stores user inputs, fixtures, expected behavior, and slice metadata.
scripts/app_target.ts calls the real answer path with fixtures.
promptfooconfig.yaml declares providers, prompts, tests, and assertions.
docs/eval-triage.md says who owns failures and waivers.

blocks.title: Harness artifact
blocks.prompt: What makes an eval harness reviewable?

options.text: A one-off notebook screenshot.
A clear file layout, target behavior, owners, and rerunnable command.
Only a vague helpfulness rubric.

blocks.explanation: A harness should be rerunnable by the team and tied to release decisions.

modules.title: Connect promptfoo to the real app path
modules.sub: Test the same routing, retrieval, and formatting users rely on.
modules.summary: The target should call the app boundary or a faithful fixture-backed slice.
objectives: Choose between direct provider prompts and custom app targets.
Use fixtures for retrieval and account state.
Avoid testing a prompt path that production never uses.

blocks.title: The target is the realism dial

spans.text: promptfoo can compare prompts directly, but a product harness often needs to call the real app path: route classification, retrieval fixtures, prompt rendering, model call, output parser, and citation validator. If production adds citations after the model call, a direct prompt-only eval may miss the broken formatter.

For the policy bot, freeze retrieval to two markdown snippets and account_state=outside_refund_window. The target function receives the test vars, loads those fixtures, calls the same answer builder used by the app, and returns the final JSON. This preserves realism while avoiding live database drift during CI.

modules.title: Encode golden cases and assertions
modules.sub: Cases should make expected behavior machine-checkable.
modules.summary: The core harness is a set of golden cases with hard and semantic checks.
objectives: Write golden cases with vars, fixtures, and metadata.
Pair each case with deterministic assertions.
Add one rubric for quality after hard checks.

blocks.title: Goldens are product expectations in miniature

spans.text: A golden case is not just an input. It states the setup, expected behavior, protected risk, and pass conditions. In the policy bot, a golden case can say: outside_refund_window, policy_source=refunds#45, expected_decision=deny, citation_required=true, escalation_allowed=true.

cells.text: deny automatic refund and cite policy
ask for review or tool result

modules.title: Run, inspect, and fail CI on regressions
modules.sub: The harness should produce a clear failure story.
modules.summary: A CI eval needs deterministic output, budget limits, and actionable failure reports.
objectives: Read a small assertion script used by promptfoo.
Predict a failing case from a missing citation.
Add a verify-AI checklist for generated harnesses.

blocks.title: Custom assertion helper for harness output

spans.text: This kind of helper can be referenced from a promptfoo assertion. It makes product rules explicit instead of hoping a broad rubric catches them.

predictThenReveal.prompt: Predict the returned reason for an outside_refund_window case with decision="approve" and no citations.
predictThenReveal.answer: The helper fails with two reasons: missing required citation and outside-window case cannot approve automatic refund. That is the release-blocking behavior the harness exists to catch.

spans.text: Checklist: the CI command uses the intended config; custom assertion files are committed with tests; fixture data is stable; failures include case ID and slice; model/provider names are pinned for the run; cost budget is explicit; and critical failures block release rather than only printing a report.

modules.title: Promote failures and tune thresholds
modules.sub: A harness stays useful only if the dataset evolves carefully.
modules.summary: The maintenance loop turns incidents into cases and stale cases into reviewed changes.
objectives: Avoid overfitting the prompt to the current test pack.

blocks.title: The harness is a living release gate

spans.text: When a production incident appears, add the smallest redacted case that would have caught it. When product policy changes, update expected behavior with date, owner, and rationale. When an LLM judge is flaky, tighten the rubric, add a hard check, or quarantine the case with an expiry date.
The harness should not overfit prompts to six examples. Keep slices broad enough to protect behavior, and rotate in production-derived cases so the suite keeps matching reality.

blocks.ruleOfThumb: A passing harness is evidence for this release, not proof of universal quality.
blocks.useWhen: Use it to block known regressions, compare release candidates, and document risk acceptance.
blocks.avoidWhen: Avoid treating a small golden set as a benchmark or ignoring failures because they are inconvenient.

blocks.title: Harness maintenance
blocks.prompt: What should happen after a production failure that the harness missed?

options.text: Delete similar tests because they were incomplete.
Add a minimal redacted case that would have caught the failure.
Only increase the model temperature.

blocks.explanation: Missed incidents are raw material for better regression coverage.

prototype.label: Prototype
prototype.laymanDefinition: A narrow build slice that proves one behavior before full production hardening.
prototype.technicalNote: A prototype should include the smallest runnable path, its failure test, and the evidence needed to decide the next build step.

retriever.label: Retriever
retriever.laymanDefinition: A component that selects candidate context or records for a question.
retriever.technicalNote: Retrievers need source IDs, filters, top-k choices, and evaluation because missing evidence changes every downstream answer.

validator.label: Validator
validator.laymanDefinition: A deterministic or model-assisted check that accepts, rejects, or repairs an output.
validator.technicalNote: Validators protect contracts such as schema, citations, allowed tools, approval rules, and safety policy.

trace.label: Trace
trace.laymanDefinition: A structured record of one run, including spans, inputs, outputs, metadata, and scores.
trace.technicalNote: Traces make failures diagnosable by showing which retrieval, model, tool, or scoring step produced the result.

deployment.label: Deployment
deployment.laymanDefinition: A released runtime configuration with model, prompt, data, infrastructure, monitoring, and rollback decisions.
deployment.technicalNote: Deployment quality depends on observability, eval gates, ownership, and privacy controls, not only code running.

acceptance_test.label: Acceptance test
acceptance_test.laymanDefinition: A test that proves a feature meets its release contract.
acceptance_test.technicalNote: Acceptance tests should be tied to user-visible behavior and include critical failure cases, not just happy paths.

kb_regression_testing.title: KB: Regression Testing for Agentic Systems

finalCheck.title: Knowledge check
finalCheck.intro: A quick check across the whole lesson — pick or type your answers.

questions.prompt: Before writing a single assertion, the harness contract requires you to define ___.

options.text: The exact wording of every prompt variant
What the harness must prove and what counts as pass or fail
The CI pipeline runner and deployment target
The number of golden cases you plan to write

questions.explanation: The contract locks in the harness's purpose and pass/fail criteria first — before any assertions or prompts are written — so every later decision has a clear standard to meet.

questions.prompt: Your app retrieves documents from a vector store before calling the LLM. Which promptfoo setup best avoids testing a prompt path that production never uses?

options.text: Use a direct provider prompt that inlines sample documents as plain text
Point promptfoo at a custom app target that runs the real retrieval + LLM call, and supply retrieval state via fixtures
Mock the LLM response entirely so retrieval doesn't matter
Duplicate the retrieval logic inside the promptfoo config file

questions.explanation: A custom app target exercises the same code path production uses; fixtures supply controlled retrieval state so the test is both realistic and repeatable.

questions.prompt: In a well-structured golden case, which ordering of assertion types is correct?

options.text: Rubric (quality) checks first, then deterministic hard checks
Hard deterministic checks first, then one rubric for quality
Only rubric checks — deterministic checks are too brittle for LLM output
Deterministic checks only — rubrics introduce subjectivity and should be avoided

questions.explanation: Hard checks (exact match, contains, regex) catch clear failures cheaply; the rubric is added last to evaluate quality only after the output has already passed the objective gates.

questions.prompt: A CI run shows one case failing with the message: 'expected citation [src-42] not found in output.' What is the most likely root cause, and what is the correct next action?
questions.acceptableAnswer: The model's response is missing a required citation (src-42). The correct next action is to treat this as a real regression — investigate whether the prompt, retrieval, or model change caused the omission — and do NOT simply relax the assertion to make the test pass.
questions.explanation: A missing citation assertion flags that the output no longer meets a hard requirement; the fix is to address the underlying cause, not to weaken the check.

questions.prompt: A production incident reveals that the model occasionally drops a required disclaimer. You fix the prompt. What should you do with the failing production case?

options.text: Delete it after the fix is confirmed — it was a one-off edge case
Promote it into the golden test pack with a dated rationale, so it guards against regression
Raise the pass-rate threshold to mask the failure until the next release
Add it only to staging fixtures, not to the main harness

questions.explanation: Promoting real failures into goldens is how the test pack grows to reflect actual risk; the dated rationale records why the threshold or case exists, preventing silent removal later.
